Treasury Yields Hit New Highs as World Leaders Squabble at Fractured G-20
 
Plus, Volkswagen fights its own board in a battle to survive, and wartime ‘coffin money’ transforms Russia’s poorest regions
 
 
SAM WOLFE/REUTERS
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

When world economic leaders gather, investors expect them to coalesce around joint challenges and quell rising anxiety in global markets. Instead, this week’s G-20 finance summit in the Blue Ridge Mountains devolved into trade spats, public insults and a dust-up over a photo op.

 

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent argued that the U.S. can grow its way out of a staggering $40 trillion debt burden. But feuds over trade with Canada and Russia’s presence sidelined discussion on the economy.

 

As the meeting closed, bond markets delivered a sharp verdict, pushing the 10-year Treasury yield to its highest level since President Trump began his second term.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• Massachusetts Sen. Ed Markey easily beat back a Democratic primary challenge from Rep. Seth Moulton.

 

• The man accused of killing Charlie Kirk potentially faces the death penalty after a Utah judge ruled there was enough evidence to warrant a trial for aggravated murder.

 

• The Maldives has become a secret hub for Russian sanctions evasion.

 

• This North Carolina county is taking mug shots offline. Not everyone agrees.

 

• Trump wants big oil companies to build more refineries to bring down gasoline prices, but constructing new facilities remains a tough sell for the industry.

 

• After a summer of long security and passport lines, our travel columnist offers a guide to sorting out the key differences between fast-pass options.

 
 
 

3. LIVE FROM THE MARKETS

• Google’s AI-research unit is set to release a new model with significantly upgraded coding capabilities, potentially shoring up an area where the company has lagged behind its competitors.

 

• Elon Musk wants to make power-turbine components, but it won’t be easy, writes Jinjoo Lee.

 
 
 

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

Volkswagen fights Chinese competition—and its own board—in a battle to survive.

 

When Volkswagen Chief Executive Oliver Blume took a cost-cutting plan to his board that envisioned doubling job losses to 100,000, he was fully aware it would be rejected. Such is the predicament of running Germany’s premier industrial company, where half the supervisory-board directors are worker representatives and swing votes are held by the local government. Now Blume is considering an audacious workaround, according to people familiar with his plans. If the board factions can’t agree, he could bypass the board and take the plan directly to shareholders. It’s a nuclear option, and the stakes are enormous, reports Stephen Wilmot.

 
 
 

5. REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK

 

Reporter Doug Belkin: Over the 14 years I’ve covered higher education, I’ve watched the public’s frustration with colleges and universities rise from low simmer to high boil—and seen the sector’s attitude migrate from denial that it had a problem to something approaching alarm.

 

Syracuse has been more transparent than most in grappling with the challenges facing higher education. A note from its president earlier this summer urging the campus community not to panic after an enrollment decline caught our eye.

 

My colleague Roshan Fernandez and I reached out to dozens of Syracuse employees, students and alumni as well as a coterie of outside higher-education experts to develop a picture of what was happening inside and outside the school.

 

The new president, Michael Haynie, is addressing Syracuse’s challenges with unusual candor. When we spoke last month, he said parents are telling him graduates aren’t ready for the world.

 

A former U.S. Air Force officer turned business professor focused on disruption, Haynie says character and resilience will be central to Syracuse moving forward: “We want to be a school that prepares you for the world’s hard edges.”

 

I’ve heard from hundreds of readers who expressed surprise that anyone would pay nearly $400,000 for an undergraduate degree. Most believe a reckoning for higher ed is at hand—and that those hard edges may be coming to college campuses next. What lies ahead is shaping up to be higher education’s most dynamic moment in a century.

6. SEE THE STORY

 

Far from the front, war cash is changing everyday life in remote Russian cities.

 
 
PHOTO ILLUSTRATION: JUNE BANG
 

In Russia’s Ulan-Ude, high sign-on bonuses and so-called “coffin money”—the payout benefits for fallen soldiers—are fueling an economic boom. New apartments, businesses and cars are appearing while graves are piling up in the local cemetery. This video offers an inside look at how front-line cash is transforming the city’s impoverished economy.

 
 
 

7. HAPPENING TODAY

 

• Second-round play begins at the U.S. Open.

 

• Economic data: The Federal Reserve releases its Beige Book, offering a ground-level snapshot of how local economies are faring and fresh clues on the central bank’s interest-rate trajectory.

8. THE NUMBER

 
0.5%
 

The alcohol by volume contained in most top nonalcoholic U.S. beer brands, according to Athletic Brewing co-founder and CEO Bill Shufelt. As sales of alternatives surge, the presence of trace alcohol is pushing consumers and industry officials to seek greater clarity around labels like “nonalcoholic,” “alcohol-free” and “zero-proof.”

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

He was a washed-up pop star. Now he’s selling out stadiums hosting baby raves.

 

Covered in tattoos, with his hair in a long braid, 35-year-old Australian DJ and former boy-band member Lenny Pearce looks more like an all-night raver than a children’s host. But he has turned his remixes of classic nursery rhymes into a global touring sensation. After giving “Head, Shoulders, Knees and Toes” a heavy techno beat, a video of Pearce rocking out to his remix went viral. A promoter pitched him on headlining a series of morning family concerts—and Australian dates sold out in days.

• Opinion: Hurray for the bond market, as investors awake at long last from nearly two decades of financial repression. Spendthrift governments might finally have to pay more to borrow and tighten their belts as a result.
